definition: This section specifies that sequence, which it calls the tail throughout.
note: Used 20 times, from §11.6 onward, before §12.4 defines it. Gloss: the ordered shutdown sequence every stop takes: wake waits, unblock devices, exit loop bodies, join under join_timeout.

definition: A *door* is an entry point that builds a run, and there are four, `init!`, `overlay!`, `restore!` and `replay!`.
note: Used in §9.2 and §11.5 before the §12.6 definition and in Appendix B. Gloss: an entry point that builds a run; the four are init!, overlay!, restore! and replay!.

definition: Every attached device receives the same handle. The handle carries the two primitive capabilities, read and stage, plus control access
note: Used across chapters 12 and 13 and Appendix B; no anchor, only a passing mention in g-snapshot. Gloss: the value attach! returns; carries read, stage and control access for one device.

definition: The levels doctrine says that **staged values are levels, never deltas**
note: Inventory bucket B points at an owning entry that does not exist in Appendix D; 10 uses incl. 'levels, never deltas'. Gloss: staged values are absolute levels, never deltas, so they are idempotent and survive coalescing.

definition: Every device's surface is its claim set, and a claim set has two sources
note: Same concept as the claim (the set of faces a device may write); alias.

definition: a claim set has two sources: A *returned* claim is enumerated by the binding ... A *computed* claim is computed by the framework at attach, when the binding declares `is_greedy(b) = true`
note: Seven uses in three sections; appD only mentions it inside g-greedy-claim. Gloss: how a claim set is obtained: returned by claims(b), or computed by the framework as the unclaimed complement under is_greedy.

definition: The binding rule states that **nothing reachable from a published snapshot is ever written again**
note: Reused in §11.8 as a name; collides with the unrelated g-binding, so the entry needs a distinct headword. Gloss: nothing reachable from a published snapshot is ever written again.

definition: the fingerprint (the structural layout)
note: Used in 16 lines across chapters 11, 12, 14 and both appendices; appD mentions it only in passing. Gloss: the store layout, root-input faces and by-position copy layout the Build fixes; replay and restore compare it.

definition: The start of a frame is its frame top.
note: Defined outside my range at §2.1; 70 uses over the body and appD has no entry (g-frame lacks the phrase). Gloss: the start of a frame, where the loop drains and reads the control plane.

definition: Attach and detach are stopped-sim operations.
note: Adjective for operations and services legal outside a running loop; heavily used, never defined in prose, may fold into g-service-lifecycle as a sense. Gloss: legal only when no loop runs: built, initialized or stopped.

definition: The heartbeat rides in the same diagnostic cell, as an atomic timestamp field
note: Used in nine sections, far from §11.8; appD covers it only inside g-diagnostic-cell. Gloss: the atomic liveness timestamp a device's handle primitives store in its diagnostic cell; stale means over 2 s behind wall clock.

definition: The run's first snapshot and its terminal snapshot ([§12.4], [§13.5]) survive any `log_every` and any `log_max`
note: Eleven uses; also spelled 'final snapshot' in §12.4. appD mentions it once in passing. Gloss: the last snapshot of a run, published before the sticky stopped status, carrying cumulative diagnostic counters.

definition: Per writer, the tail residue is the final ring and its suppressed counts.
note: Defined in §11.8, used in §12.4, §13.5 and Appendix C. Gloss: what the tail's last pass over the diagnostic cells collects after the terminal snapshot; folded into the termination record, never published.

definition: The run's-end sweep, the loop's last pass over every diagnostic cell
note: Five uses over three sections; pairs with tail residue and could share one entry. Gloss: the loop's last pass over every diagnostic cell, collecting the tail residue into the termination record.

definition: Only then does it set the sticky stopped status.
note: Five uses in three sections, never defined in prose; mentioned in appD without an entry. Gloss: the Control flag the tail sets after the terminal snapshot; it stays set until the next door clears it.

definition: The snapshot carries the trajectory's *published-boundary ordinal* with `t`.
note: Defined in §10.4 (outside my range) and restated in §12.3; one of three indices §12.3 separates from the boundary counter and the frame-entry boundary index. Gloss: the count of publications in a trajectory, 0 at boundary zero, carried by each snapshot.

definition: a third index, the frame-entry boundary index of [§13.4], a frame count that names no `t*` boundary
note: Nine uses across four sections; used by replay pointers and error messages. Gloss: a count of frame tops naming a frame entry; the index replay!(to_boundary=k) and StepError use.

definition: A deep path is an *inspection* read ... An exported output face, spelled `get_face(name)`, is an *integration* read.
note: Used far from §11.2 (§8.6, §13.3, §14.4). Gloss: an inspection read uses deep paths, no promises; an integration read goes through a named, curated, meaning-stable face.

definition: an attach-compiled *scatter*, which maps position → root-input cell, statically typed ... the exact mirror of the compiled output gather
note: Output gather and input scatter used in §11.2, §11.4, §11.6, §12.7 and §14.4; they name the two halves of attach-time compilation. Gloss: the attach-compiled reads of a binding's selectors (gather) and writes of a batch to root-input cells (scatter).

definition: The shim does three things. It maps name to position, converts to the root input's declared type, and sets the mask.
note: Five uses in three sections, all inside chapter 11; demote to D if local gloss suffices. Gloss: the attach-compiled conversion that turns face => value pairs into a positional batch with a touched mask.

definition: Its type declares which sides it has and enumerates what each side touches.
note: Input side and output side, declared by is_input/is_output; 'declared side' used in §14.7 and §14.8 too. Gloss: the input or output half of a binding, declared by a trait and checked against its claims or reads method.

definition: The port view is this section's baked verdict, one per declared port of every component, input and output.
note: Used in §9.2 and Appendix B, far from §11.7. Gloss: the per-port record port_views builds: terminal producer, liveness verdict, staging slot and incumbent writer.

definition: the incumbent writer of a root-driven port the GUI does not command
note: Thirteen uses, a role name in diagnostics and port views; ordinary English, so a one-line gloss may do. Gloss: the device whose claim covers a root-input face, or the harness writer when no device claims it.

definition: The loop catches it at one of its unmask points, where a deferred Ctrl-C is raised
note: Three uses in sections 12.1, 12.4, 13.4 (the §10.7 and §11.4 hits are other senses). Gloss: a boundary-consistent point where the loop re-enables SIGINT delivery: frame top, wait and pause blocks.

definition: It is the state what-if, the sibling of the input what-if, which is a restore followed by `stage!`
note: Names the overlay! workflow; two of three uses are in appendices. 'input what-if' is an alias of g-what-if-replay or restore plus stage!. Gloss: overlay! of a condition onto a stopped run, continued as a fresh trajectory.

definition: A *complete* writer covers every face in every batch it stages ... A *sparse* writer stages only what was touched.
note: All uses in §11.4; inline gloss only.

definition: One device contract means author-owned loop bodies.
note: All five uses sit in §11.6 beside the definition.

definition: Spawn-inside-`run!` is the start gate
note: One use.

definition: one spawned task per rostered device, all run-scoped
note: Ordinary adjective for per-run lifetime; three uses, two sections.

definition: Diagnostic sites follow the compilation, every one of them to staging
note: Two uses, one section.

definition: A `Simulation` is constructed with a placeholder run
note: Two uses, one section.

definition: The derived/primary split ([D-038]) decides why decimation is admissible here and not there.
note: One use; 'division of labor' (§11.2:7082) is a second one-use coinage of D-038.

definition: `log_max` is a view policy, not a trajectory-determining one
note: One use.

definition: Re-decimation, like decimation, loses *which* boundary within a stretch an occurrence fell on
note: One use; covered by g-decimation's sense.

definition: A stepping session is deviceless by construction
note: Three uses, two sections, next to the definition; 'harness mode' (two uses) is its alias.

definition: under [the roster freeze](#g-the-freeze) (attach and detach only while stopped, below)
note: Already linked to g-the-freeze in the text; nine uses of 'the freeze'.

definition: Staging has one coalescing policy, CAS merge, newest wins per face
note: Same policy as coalescing; 'newest-wins' in §12.3 is its outbound mirror (g-next-snapshot-wait).

definition: A deviceless run is the harness and CI mode
note: Near-synonym of unattended run (empty staging, no readers); a run with no rostered device.

definition: The stop policy is declared per advance
note: Prose name for the StopPolicy value.
